Our goal is to estimate these rates from data collected before the onset of an epidemic, with the aim of improving contact tracing efforts and public health policies.  We develop a new Bayesian inference approach called "Sleepless Inference" that enables us to model age-specific rates of infection and recovery simultaneously, allowing for smooth transitions between these rates when moving from one age group to the next.  Our results indicate that Sleepless Inference outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and consistency, reducing overall uncertainty by at least 30\% in most cases.  We also find that modeling transmission and recovery rates jointly results in more plausible estimates, especially for younger age groups.  Finally, we apply Sleepless Inference to real-world data from the 2014-2016 West African Ebola outbreak and the 2020-2021 Indian COVID-19 wave, demonstrating its effectiveness in various scenarios. We conclude that Sleepless Inference offers a versatile and efficient framework for incorporating prior knowledge into statistical models, enabling researchers to recover underlying patterns from noisy data. This result signifies that the shape theorem holds for the original walk without the need for the usual growth condition. ion points in elliptic curves over the field of rational numbers when scaled by a power of a prime number.  Following an approach by Koblitz, we examine how points of finite order on an elliptic curve over the rational numbers, when scaled by a power of a prime number, relate to points of finite order on a reduced curve with integral coordinates.  We derive conditions for a point to be a quadratic torsion point on a scaled elliptic curve, as well as its preimage on the unscaled curve.  These conditions enable us to classify possible quadratic torsion points on scaled elliptic curves over the rational numbers, in the absence of a general algorithm for computing all points of finite order on an elliptic curve over the rationals.  This classification is consistent with existing knowledge regarding quadratic residues and reciprocity laws.  Furthermore, we observe that certain infinitely numerous sets of positive integers, when squared and considered modulo a prime number of at least 5, correspond to points of finite order on some elliptic curve over the rational numbers when scaled by a power of that prime number.  These sets include squares that are second-power free, squares of first-power free numbers, and certain sequences defined by Clausen and Eisen.  Additionally, we discover that certain infinitely numerous sets of positive integers, when squared and considered modulo a prime number, correspond to preimages of quadratic torsion points on some elliptic curve over the rational numbers when scaled by a power of that prime number.  These sets include residues and nonresidues of a number when squared and considered modulo a prime number of at least 3, squares that are second-power free, squares of first-power free numbers, and certain sequences defined by Clausen and Eisen.  These findings contribute to our understanding of points of finite order on elliptic curves over the rational numbers when scaled by a power of a prime number.  It is notable that all previously known cases of point multiplication phenomena, involving a prime number as a factor, fall within these classifications.  These phenomena include Wile's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, Mordell's Conjecture (proven by Shaferevich for a specific case of a curve over a number field with a finite rank), the Anomaly of the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture for an infinitely numerous set of examples, and the No-Elliptic Curve Theorem for a finite number of prime numbers (extendable to all prime numbers greater than 20'000). to utilize imaging studies for both initial patient segmentation and ongoing monitoring.  This unique property sets biometric imaging study based clinical trials apart from other data-driven clinical trials, and yields several benefits and drawbacks.  On the positive side, starting with a clear image of the affected area can enhance the power of statistical tests, allowing for more diverse patient populations to benefit from these trials.  Additionally, existing infrastructure in hospitals to conduct and analyze imaging studies can be leveraged, potentially reducing costs and expediting the trial process.  However, utilizing imaging studies also introduces complexity and raises several technical challenges that must be addressed.  Perhaps the most significant of these challenges is developing accurate and automated methods to outline the affected area from imaging studies, a task known as segmentation.  Without reliable segmentation methods, trial designers risk compromising the validity of statistical inferences and the trial's overall integrity.  In this paper, we explore the advantage of biometric imaging study based clinical trials and the difficulty of achieving suitable segmentation outcomes.  We begin by outlining several key properties that suitable segmentation methods should exhibit, including accuracy, efficiency, and consistency, before delving into a variety of challenges that typically arise when assessing these properties.  We also discuss various solutions to these challenges across multiple topics, including validation methods, optimization approaches, and modeling assumptions.  By better understanding these challenges and their solutions, researchers can develop more effective ways to achieve reliable segmentation outcomes, enabling these trials to fully realize their potential and contribute significantly to medical knowledge.  Ultimately, we argue that validation is an ongoing process that trial designers should commit to pursuing regularly throughout the trial's duration, in addition to participating in preliminary experiments before the trial begins.  By doing so, they can guarantee the integrity of the trial and ensure the validity of statistical inferences.  We conclude by outlining several areas where researchers can improve existing segmentation methods and explore new alternatives, including deep learning techniques, semi-supervised approaches, and multiple scanner formats.  We hope that this paper serves as a comprehensive guide for trial designers, statisticians, and analysts to develop reliable segmentation methods that yield valid results and contribute significantly to medical knowledge.  We also hope that it inspires researchers to explore novel ideas and alternatives that can be applied to real-world scenarios.  As biometric imaging study based clinical trials continue to grow in number, we expect them to influence how segmentation methods are developed and validated across multiple fields, including neuroscience, oncology, and cardiology.  By doing so, they can lead to breakthroughs in our understanding of various diseases and conditions

of a conjecture by Blass, that a Boolean algebra is representable in a finite dimension d if and only if it is (bd)-free, where (bd) is the combinatorial structure known as the 'binary decomposition property'. The proof is based on an initial-part invariant within such representable Boolean algebras, which can be shown to be equivalent to the absence of (bd) by using a result by R. J. Galicer. The final part of the proof involves demonstrating that the initial-part invariant is cumulative when combining two (bd)-free Boolean algebras in a join-complementable way, which can then be transformed into a structure known as a 'tree-decomposition' via a process called 'unfolding'. The tree-decomposition can be utilized to prove that the product of two (bd)-free Boolean algebras is (td<sub>3</sub>)-free, which then enables the application of a known result by F. Galvin and A. Tarski. The overall line of reasoning enables the verification that a Boolean algebra is d-representable if and only if it is (td<sub>3</sub>)-free for any natural number d. The proof's structure is reflective of a general strategy for extending results from finite dimensions to infinite dimensions. The final part of the abstract mentions that the proved conjecture is equivalent to a combination of conditions concerning the presence of tree-decompositions of width 3, which can be replaced by conditions concerning the presence of 'binary decomposition properties' of order d for any natural number d. The abstract concludes by highlighting the theorem's implications on the conservation of first-order properties between the class of d-representable Boolean algebras and the class of (td<sub>3</sub>)-free Boolean algebras for any natural number d. Theoretical models predicting this state rely on an assumption that the superfluid's vortices exhibit non-abelian statistics, a property confirmed by a quantum phase transition in a related model. We show that any streaming algorithm that uses a constant amount of space and is genuinely interactive (i.e., requires interaction with the data to make decisions) cannot be fully accurate and robust when faced with an adversary who can amend the input stream and the outputs of the algorithm.  This restriction holds even when the algorithm knows the underlying distribution of the data in advance.  If the algorithm is pre-trained, then an algorithm with limited comparison capabilities (e.g., comparison to a fixed number) cannot be fully accurate and robust.  If the algorithm can compare to anything that it has seen before, then an algorithm with unlimited comparison capabilities cannot be fully accurate and robust unless it has a significant amount of space at its disposal (i.e., nearly linear space).  All of these bounds are achievable by specific algorithms.  These results stem from a more general fact that any streaming algorithm that uses a constant amount of space and is genuinely interactive cannot distinguish extremely rare and extremely common events unless the events differ significantly in probability (i.e., have an exponential difference).  These findings have implications for the study of streaming algorithms, particularly those employed in statistical learning and property testing.  They also contribute to our understanding of the fundamental limitations of algorithms when confronted with uncertain and unpredictable circumstances.  These circumstances arise in various domains including machine learning, data science, and computational complexity.  These results may influence the development of future algorithms and the way we think about the boundaries of algorithmic capability.  They demonstrate that the effectiveness of algorithms can be impaired by the simplest changes in scenario or context.  They showcase the importance of considering the conditions and environment in which algorithms operate. Building on our previous finding that a constant anisotropic stress is not compatible with gravitational wave generation in the early universe, we demonstrate that a linear anisotropic stress is insufficient for significant gravitational wave production. This minimum value is found to be proportional to the amplitude of the anisotropic stress, with a constant of proportionality dependent on the speed of sound in the anisotropic sector. we develop a polynomial time algorithm to solve quaternion congruence problems, specifically to find the smallest positive integer power of a given quaternion that matches a predetermined target quaternion.  This solution extends the existing solutions for complex congruence problems in matrices to quaternion congruence problems and also generalizes the existing solutions for real congruence problems in matrices to quaternion congruence problems.  Our approach utilizes Moebius transformation techniques, particularly applying a recursive formula that solves generalized left-linear Diophantine systems, and we also include an efficient method for solving generalized left-linear Diophantine systems with rational coefficients.  Our solution for the quaternion congruence problem involves solving these types of Diophantine systems as well as performing matrix operations, and we demonstrate its applicability in solving complex congruence problems in matrices by extending the solution to include negative integer exponents.  Our algorithm is validated through a theoretical analysis of its time complexity, and we provide a concise summary of the overall approach.  We apply the quaternion congruence problem solution in various scenarios, including developing a polynomial time algorithm for verifying the positive definiteness of matrix-valued polynomials, solving homogeneous linear equations with matrix variables, and validating the positive definiteness of matrix polynomial combinations. The solution's applicability extends to other types of periodic symmetric matrices, including Hermitian matrices, symmetric matrices, and matrix-valued polynomials, and we demonstrate its utility in several examples. We demonstrate that any such periodic trajectory is either an altitude or a variant of an altitude after possible transformation of the triangle's shape.  This conclusion applies to both visible and invisible trajectories.  This comprehensive theorem simplifies the classification of periodic trajectories on an isosceles oblique hyperbolic triangle, leaving three distinct types: altitudes, (√t-1)/2 shaped curves when t ≠ 1, and a special case when t = 1.  This classification is a preliminary step towards our main contribution, which presents a detailed analysis of the dynamics of a periodic trajectory by substituting time (mod Λ) with a new parameter (s).  This new parameter enables the calculation of the total variation of a trajectory's width, allowing for the determination of a trajectory's extremal properties.  Our research reveals that any closed and periodic trajectory's maximum width can be found by optimizing the value of t.  This optimization process involves solving a coefficient-free inequality for a monic quadratic polynomial.  We conclude by outlining future research directions on the topic of closed and periodic trajectories on an isosceles oblique hyperbic triangle.  One proposed area of exploration involves the investigation of the closed and periodic trajectory with the smallest possible total variation, all while assuming a triangle angle of π/3.  Another proposed area of exploration involves the research of closed and periodic trajectories on a triangle with a right angle, which can be thought of as a limit case of an isosceles hyperbolic triangle.  We also suggest the study of the closed and periodic trajectory with the smallest possible total variation on a triangle with a right angle, as well as the investigation of the closed and periodic trajectory with the largest possible width on a triangle with a right angle.  Additionally, we propose the examination of the closed and periodic trajectory's extremal properties on a triangle with a right angle, all while exploring the possibility of a first-order differential equation that describes the dynamics of a closed and periodic trajectory on a right-angled triangle.

A key aspect of this construction is the ordering of the devices based on the SINR values obtained when they receive signals from each pair of devices in the group.  A polynomial-time algorithm has been developed to achieve this ordering for a group of n devices when the group's configuration is a tree or when the group's configuration is a forest consisting of at most two connected components.  This algorithm utilizes a variant of Fomin's parameterized algorithm for searching for weakly exponentially bounded WHIN-free patterns.  It also utilizes a straightforward greedy algorithm to order the devices based on the visible set visible(S) of each device S.  The visible set visible(S) consists of all real values alpha for which there exists a schedule that yields an SINR value greater than alpha at device S under the given noise and interference levels when signals from other devices interfere as noise.  The total time required to execute this algorithm under the mentioned conditions is bounded by O(n^7) in the worst case.  Additionally, the algorithm's efficiency is demonstrated through an example where a group of 10 devices is arranged in a regular 3-dimensional grid.  In this example, the total time required to execute the algorithm is less than 2 seconds.  It is also shown that an ordering that optimizes the SINR values at the devices can be obtained in general in O(n^10) time by removing the restriction on the configuration's connectivity.  It is also noted that optimizing the visible set visible(S) directly is computationally challenging; it is shown that determining whether the largest possible value of the largest visible set visible_max is greater than a given real value delta is equivalent to solving a weakly exponentially bounded first-order spectrum problem. Precision calculation of this time delay is complex, involving various factors such as the gravitational wave signal parameters, the position of the observer, and the binary system's distance.  A team of researchers has developed an efficient method for computing the time delay between gravitational wave observations and electromagnetic follow-up visions of binary black hole merger events. The team envisions this precomputed database being available publicly, enabling the quick calculation of time delays for various parameters and viewpoints, and facilitating the follow-up vision of binary black hole merger events with electromagnetic telescopes.  This research contributes to the development of various search methods for binary black hole mergers, incorporating the time delay into physical models, and enabling the inclusion of follow-up vision constraints in search algorithms.  This research also paves the way for the participation of wide-field radio telescopes in the search for binary black hole merger events. While optical and gamma-ray emissions in these objects are well-explained by synchrotron radiation, X-ray observations often yield higher energies than expected, leading some to propose an inner jet component responsible for these X-rays or a different emission mechanism such as inverse Compton radiation from a relativistic pair flux.  Using the most precise data available for the X-ray rich Blazar 3C 454.3, we demonstrate that an increase in amplitude and a shift in peak energy of the X-ray spectrum occur when the source's Lorentz factor beta_0 approximates 10, eliminating the need for an inner jet or pair flux.  This finding is consistent with a constant external radiation energy density influencing the X-ray emission through both acceleration and cooling processes.  By applying a simple power-law model to the spectrum and assuming a jet power of 10^28 erg/s, we derive an electron energy distribution that lacks a gap, eliminating the possibility of gamma-ray absorption.  However, observation of this source in gamma-rays is crucial to verify this theory.  As this analysis is focused on a single, extreme event, further observations of similar events are necessary to confirm these results.  Additionally, a larger sample of Blazar X-ray spectra is needed to determine if this behavior is unique to 3C 454.3 or a common property of these objects.  If verified, this discovery could pave the way for a unified theory of Blazar emission mechanisms.  Furthermore, as 3C 454.3 is an extreme case, its characteristics may serve as a laboratory to test extreme relativistic jet theory in the most severe conditions possible.  Finally, if a population of similar sources exists, it could significantly impact our understanding of powerful radio-loud AGNs and their role in shaping the large-scale structure of the universe.  Ultimately, this research highlights the important role that precise X-ray and gamma-ray observations play in shaping our understanding of the most powerful extragalactic sources in the universe.  As these sources are extremely rare and distant, precise data from the next generation of X-ray and gamma-ray telescopes will be crucial in advancing our knowledge of these objects.  Moreover, the development of more sensitive instruments is necessary to study the X-ray and gamma-ray behavior of even closer and more common Blazars, allowing us to better comprehend the physical processes that shape their emission mechanisms. These networks often evolve over time, influencing how information spreads and is organized within the system.  As these systems grow and change, they shape the way information diffuses through the network, ultimately influencing its structure.  In return, the way information moves through the network impacts how parts of the network develop and evolve over time.  This reciprocal relationship is the focus of this talk, exploring how information diffusion drives network evolution and how a network's structure affects the spread of information within it.  We investigate this interplay using a simple model of local information encounters and a growth model for network evolution. Additionally, we investigate how the distribution of information correlates with network properties such as size, component size, and the number of nodes with high degree.  We apply this model to various examples of information spreads, including wave propagation, concentration gradients, and the spread of knowledge in a population of individuals with varying levels of influence.  We demonstrate that certain patterns of information diffusion can lead to the formation of complex network structures and vice versa.  This research contributes to our understanding of how information drives network evolution and how newly evolving structures impact the spread of information within the system.  We apply this framework to various systems, including biological, physical, and technological examples, and propose its utilization in fields such as biology, physics, and economics. of infinitely many prime numbers that are congruent to 113 modulo a small power of 2. Specifically, we show that there are infinitely many prime numbers that are congruent to 113 modulo $2^5$. This finding is a part of a larger series of primes that are congruent to 113 modulo a power of 2, following the pattern observed by Bachet in the 17th century. Building upon the work by Bachet, we extend the sequence to include primes that are congruent to 113 modulo $2^n$ for n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. We achieve this by developing a recursive formula that enables the generation of these primes in a structured manner. The formula's geometric interpretation reveals that it corresponds to a crystal-like shape within a 2D lattice, allowing us to utilize tools from number theory, geometry, and discrete mathematics to prove the existence of these primes. The underlying structure also enables us to calculate the density of these primes within the range of numbers from 1 to N for a given value of N. The overall result contributes to our understanding of prime number distribution and its unique pattern when congruent to 113 modulo a power of 2. Through microwave generation of spin waves, we have successfully induced these massive oscillations in a YIG/Permalloy system, allowing us to study their characteristics for the first time.  By analyzing the SQR and FMR spectra, we found that spin-Hall ferromagnetic resonance occurs when the microwave field aligns spin waves with the pre-existing magnetization, all while ignoring the 2DEG's contribution to the total magnetization.  Furthermore, our research revealed that this new type of oscillation behaves identically to traditional FMR in terms of its theoretical model, confirming that it is merely a perspective based on the 2DEG's spin-Hall effect.  To further explore the properties of spin-Hall ferromagnetic resonance, we conducted experiments with different pre-alignment angles and spin wave amplitudes, observing no influence of these factors on the oscillation amplitude while noting a direct proportionality with the spin wave amplitude.  Additionally, our research showed that the gyration velocity of these oscillations matches that of traditional FMR, along with exhibiting similar decay behavior in the presence of spin wave damping.  Ultimately, our experimental findings align with a theoretical model that treats spin-Hall ferromagnetic resonance as traditional FMR, with the 2DEG's spin-Hall effect acting as an observable manifestation of the spin wave circulation pattern.  This research demonstrates the possibility of manipulating large amplitude spin-Hall oscillations through spin wave generation, opening up the potential for utilizing this new type of magnetization oscillation in various applications.  One such possible application is the development of high-performance microwave detectors, which could offer improved sensitivity by exploiting the large amplitude oscillations and strong coupling between spin waves and microwaves in the system.  Another possible application is the use of spin-Hall ferromagnetic resonance in high-performance magnetic imaging techniques, allowing for the visualization of spin wave distribution patterns within the system.  Lastly, our research suggests the viability of employing spin-Hall ferromagnetic resonance in the creation of high-efficiency microwave sources, which could offer enhanced performance by utilizing the large amplitude oscillations and strong spin wave-microwave coupling in the system.  This research paves the way for exploring the theoretical limits of spin-Hall ferromagnetic resonance, as well as investigating its behavior in various systems and configurations

  sparked intense interest. These anomalies, involving the $D^{*0}\ell^-$ final state,
  consist of decreases in $R_K$ and $R_{D^{*0}}$ when comparing ratios that include
  muons versus electrons. These decreases are small, making precise measurements crucial.
  Based on 2.0 $\lhd$ 2.6 $fb^{-1}$ of LEP data, we have made precise measurements of
  $R_K$, $R_{eD^{*0}}$, and $R_{\mu D^{*0}}$. These quantities represent ratios of
  $B^0 \rightarrow D^{*0} \ell \bar{\nu}$ decay branching fractions with different lepton
  species. Our findings of $R_K = 29.5 \pm 0.6 \pm 0.8 \pm 0.5$, $R_{eD^{*0}} = 3.69 \pm
  0.13 \pm 0.16 \pm 0.05$, and $R_{\mu D^{*0}} = 9.5 \pm 0.4 \pm 0.5 \pm 0.3$ agree
  with theoretical predictions. Our measurements contribute to the overall evidence for
  lepton-flavor universality and its non-universality when comparing electrons and muons.
  Our findings also meet the requirements for furthering discussion on the possible
  interpretations of these anomalies.  As our results stand, we see no evidence for a new
  physics sector in $B^0 \rightarrow D^{*0} \ell \bar{\nu}$ decays. However, our measurements

The new trigger system consists of two levels: the hardware trigger level and the software trigger level.  In the hardware trigger level, a fast approximation of jet p_T is calculated using fewer than 10% of the total proton-proton collision data.  This approximation enables the selection of collisions with the highest jet p_T, thereby reducing data that require further processing.  The software trigger level, on the other hand, utilizes the full proton-proton collision data to calculate the jet p_T more precisely.  This more precise measurement allows for more stringent jet p_T criteria to be applied.  We have successfully tested the new trigger system using various data samples, including those with high-energy jets and those with little to no energy transferred to particles detected in the forward direction.  The results obtained indicate that the new trigger system is efficient in identifying high-energy jets and is capable of reducing data by at least an order of magnitude compared to the existing single-layer trigger system.  We have also tested the new trigger system using various physics processes, including those with significant transverse momentum transferred to particles detected in the forward direction, without which important physics information may be lost.  The new trigger system meets the requirements for detecting physics processes that involve the transformation of energy to particles detected in the forward direction, as well as those that involve the transformation of energy to particles detected in the central region of the detector.  The new trigger system is expected to enable LHCb to make significant contributions to a wide range of physics topics, including those involving high-energy jets, energy transfer to particles detected in the forward direction, and the study of heavy-flavor quarks in beauty b-quark decay.  The development of this new trigger system paves the way for LHCb to explore uncharted areas of physics at incredibly high energies, allowing it to discover novel phenomena, verify established theories, and refine our understanding of the fundamental nature of matter.  The novel, multi-layered trigger system presented herein serves as a model for other experiments and detectors to emulate, enabling them to discover uncharted areas of physics, verify established theories, and refine our understanding of the fundamental nature of matter.

  but have been shown to be vulnerable to subtle attacks that alter only a small number
  of input coordinates. Such threats contradict the trust that's typically assumed when
  optimizing DNNs and also put sensitive information at risk. In many instances, the
  accuracy of DNNs decreases significantly when they encounter slightly distorted inputs.
  Based on the observation that natural, real-world data distributions often involve correlations
  between various input characteristics, we propose a new attack strategy called the targeted
  coordinate wise perturbation (TCP). This TCP attack methodology differs from existing
  methods in the following ways: it only modifies a limited number of input coordinates;
  it targets specific classes; it's applicable to both classification and regression DNNs;
  it works even when there's significant overlap between distinct data distributions; and
  it can effectively exploit existing regularizations that prioritize robustness. We've
  also developed a novel regularizer called the structured robustness regularizer (SRR)
  that complements the TCP attack. This SRR regularizer is designed to enhance the resilience
  of DNNs to subtle attacks and improve their accuracy when processing naturally corrupted
  inputs. Our proposed TCP attack and SRR regularizer outperformed other existing attack
  strategies and regularizers in various tests conducted on multiple public datasets.    Categories:   Artificial Intelligence;  Deep Learning;  Neural Networks;  Data Perturbations;  Attack Strategies;  Regularizers;  Robustness;  Deep Neural Networks.

Building on these findings, we develop a flexible source-wavefield compensation technique that eliminates the need for precise initial models by allowing for significant perturbations.  By comparing the results of this new technique with traditional FWI, we demonstrate its superiority in terms of convergence stability, allowing for initial model perturbations of up to 100% without distortion.  As the technique eliminates the sensitivity of FWI to initial models, we propose removing the initial model estimate and derive an automatic initialization method that promotes physical reality.  Applying this method to real and synthetic data yields high-quality inverted models with moderate to low frequency content, demonstrating its effectiveness.  As the new compensation technique offers enhanced convergence stability, we anticipate its widespread application in FWI, enabling the reconstruction of deep structure from seismic explosion data with high frequency resolution. With the development of wide-aperture seismic experimentation and the growing complexity of source designs, we expect the new technique to make a significant impact on the development of high-resolution seismic experimentation and imaging methods.   to recreate the growth process of planets within protoplanetary disks through computer
  simulations. These simulations often rely on assumptions regarding the initial conditions
  of these disks, which might affect the outcome of the results. What remains unknown

  is the observation of small, meteorite-sized particles within these disks, which can
  be detected through the way they emit radiation when colliding and heating up around
  nearby stars. These particles' sizes can provide insights into how planets form from
  small particles (pebbles) that drift towards the center of these disks under gravity.

  particles of two distinct sizes within the disk: those that orbit closer to the star

  near the disk's center that generated significant heat when colliding with each other
  and the disk's surface. The findings suggest that these massive particles might be too

This part of the scattering amplitude is known as the impact factor. Bardeen, Currie, and Tung (BCT) initially proposed this impact factor model nearly five decades ago. A fundamental aspect of this effort involves determining how local atomic levels contribute to the overall electronic structure of materials, particularly when they form complexes in solid forms.  While theoretical methods like density functional theory can calculate the isolated atomic levels of constituent elements, determining the levels of complex molecular units proves more challenging.  As a result, researchers rely on various approximations and assumptions when modelling certain materials, which can introduce uncertainty into outcomes.  To address this issue, we have developed a novel, experimental approach to directly measure the electronic levels of complex molecular units in solid materials.  By creating a gas of these units under extremely low pressure, we can apply spectroscopic methods to determine their levels before they bond together and affect the overall electronic structure of the material.  To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, we conducted a test on the silver oxide molecule (Ag2O2), a crucial component of the superconducting material beta-Ag2O2.  Our results show that the partial filling of a molecular orbital in Ag2O2 is responsible for its normal-state properties, including its conductivity and magnetic properties.  By understanding how the local levels of the Ag2O2 molecule contribute to the electronic structure of beta-Ag2O2, we can develop a more comprehensive theoretical framework for modelling similar materials with similar characteristics.  Ultimately, this framework paves the way for the design of new materials with potentially unprecedented properties.  In the case of the beta-Ag2O2 system, our findings suggest that increasing pressure on the material should enhance its superconducting temperature (Tc). observed in the microquasar V4647-020 is not a standard disc cavity, which is typically caused by a companion star's influence on the disc.  To evaluate this claim, we examine the unusual properties of the system, which includes a massive companion star and an undermassive black hole.  If the star's strong tidal forces do create the cavity, we should see a corresponding effect on the disc's hot inner region, which we define as the 'tidal heating signature.'  By analyzing multi-episodic X-ray and radio observations of the jet, we look for evidence of the star's tidal influence on the disc, which would manifest as irregularities in the disc's temperature and/or the formation of a tidal heating ring.  If the disc cavity is an unusual type, we expect to find little to no evidence of the tidal heating signature, confirming the proposed theory.  As the observations show no signs of the tidal heating signature or a heating ring, we conclude that the disc cavity in V4647-020 is an example of an 'empty cavity,' which is created when the star's strong tidal forces push some of the disc's material towards the innermost regions of the system, where it heats up and forms a hot inner disc or jet-driving region.  This finding is consistent with other systems with undermassive black holes and massive companion stars, such as GRS 1919-21 and XTE J November 13. Utilizing Wuppertofer's lattice QCD configuration generator, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of these fluctuations by collecting ~1.5 billion lattice gauge field configurations following a parallel tempering Monte Carlo simulation.  With the purpose of analyzing the fluctuations, we employed an extensive array of lattice parameters spanning a wide range of temperatures (from near zero to nearly the QCD transition temperature) and varying the lattice size to minimize finite volume effects.  A key finding is that the fluctuations in local scale and parity transformations do not exhibit a direct correlation with the underlying topology of the gauge field configurations.  Furthermore, we observed that the fluctuations in local scale transformations are significantly greater than those in local parity transformations, which we attribute to the inherent nature of scale and parity transformations rather than factors related to the Monte Carlo simulation.  Additionally, we discovered that the fluctuations in the topological charge do not align with the underlying topological class of the gauge field configurations, which we believe is a crucial aspect of the resolution of the famous 'parity problem' in QCD.  To conclude, we note that the fluctuations in local scale and parity transformations are relevant to the development of suitable order parameters that distinguish different topological sectors of lattice QCD gauge field configurations.  The research reported in this study contributes to the advancement of our understanding of QCD, particularly in regards to the role of topological properties in the formation of chiral symmetry within the theory.  The research also contributes to the development of numerical approaches for studying lattice QCD, specifically the construction of order parameters that differentiate between distinct topological sectors of the gauge field configurations. This research focuses on detoxification techniques that modify existing language models to remove toxic embeddings and those that train new models without toxic data.  We conduct an in-depth analysis of the effectiveness, fairness, and fiscal implications of these methods by conducting numerous experiments on English and non-English languages.  The results show that while detoxification techniques can effectively reduce toxic output, they often sacrifice accuracy in the process.  What's more, our findings reveal that these methods reflect the biases present in their training data, which means they work better with content created by majority language groups at the expense of minority groups.  Finally, we find that training new models without toxic data comes with significant fiscal implications.  Our research suggests that detoxification techniques are not a viable solution to creating language models that produce respectful output.  Instead, we propose an alternative approach - educating language models to produce courteous content through training with gentle feedback.  Our results demonstrate that simply using partial or hidden outputs during training can encourage language models to produce more polite responses.  What's more, we observe that pre-existing models pre-trained on large datasets also have an innate capacity to generate courteous output.  Our research provides a foundation for developing language models that produce respectful output without exposing models to toxic content in the first place.  We hope our findings will inspire the development of more ethical language models.  Our code and models are available for download at  https://github.com/ghru/LanguageModelDetoxification.   Recent experiments on the heavy-electron system CePdReO on cooling from 2 K show an unusual peak in specific heat around 0.6 K but not 0.1 K as predicted by theoretical expectations for a quantum critical point.
  To provide a more complete understanding of these results, we have performed detailed magnetic susceptibility measurements on the system, revealing an unexpected increase in the curvature of the Curie-Weiss plot around 0.6 K.
  This unexpected curvature is not thought to be caused by magnetic ordering or spin density wave behavior but rather by the system's approach to a quantum critical point along the Pd concentration axis.
  This new interpretation is consistent with the unusual peak in specific heat measurements and suggests that CePdReO is near a quantum critical point for an enhanced ferromagnetic order along the Pd concentration axis.   Research in cognitive science has shown that people quickly pick up on recurring patterns in music, yet the processes involved are not well understood.
  To better comprehend how individuals recognize and identify musical themes, an experiment used functional magnetic resonance imaging to scan the brains of 13 musicians and 12 non-musicians while playing back both familiar and unfamiliar musical themes.
  The results indicate that the same brain regions responsible for recognizing visual patterns also recognize musical patterns, suggesting that pattern recognition theory may explain how themes are identified.
  Additionally, significant differences were found between the brain activity of musicians and non-musicians when recognizing familiar themes, indicating that musical expertise influences the brain's recognition processes.
  The findings provide a neurological basis for how themes are recognized and identified in music, and offer insights for a more comprehensive pattern recognition model. 
  The research contributes to both cognitive science and music theory by providing a novel understanding of how people perceive and recognize musical structure. 
  The findings also have implications for the development of music information retrieval systems that can recognize and identify musical themes. 
  Overall, the study demonstrates the effectiveness of a combined cognitive and neuroimaging approach in understanding how people process musical structure.

This growth in expectation comes at a time when academic rewards are heavily tied to the impact factor of journals in which research is published.  In the field of artificial intelligence, with its vast potential to impact society positively or negatively, the stakes are particularly high. This is particularly true for research seeking to guide policy decisions in the AI domain.  We argue that a more nuanced approach is required that takes into account the diverse nature of research and its purposes.  We propose a multi-dimensional framework to replace the impact factor, centered around the aims of research and the influences it seeks to exert on the world.  This framework consists of four dimensions: technical influence, social impact, ethical considerations, and methodological rigor.  We further suggest that journals catering to the AI policy-making community should adopt this new framework when evaluating the value of their published research.  By doing so, they can promote a culture that prioritizes the quality of research over its impact factor, ultimately leading to more effective and responsible research that truly matters.  We illustrate the applicability of this framework by applying it to three real-world research scenarios. A reliable model is crucial for deriving conclusions from the observation of a transient's cooling behavior. We present a novel approach to analyzing transient sources' cooling curves by linking them to the neutron star's internal composition and temperature profiles. A simple parameterization allows us to model the initial transient signal and a simple analytical model enables us to predict the cooling behavior for various combinations of physical parameters. We find that the majority of these sources cannot be explained by a single composition model, instead suggesting that some transients might be composed of stars with different core structures. Additionally, we observe that the most plausible explanations for the extreme behaviors exhibited by some sources (extra cooling and non-standard heat transfers) are unlikely to occur in pure 3FLW models but could be more feasible in hybrid models that incorporate a mix of 3FLW and normal quark phases. Ultimately, we emphasize the importance of developing more accurate theoretical models of neutron star physics and the need for more sensitive observations of transient sources. grid representing a cow's field with obstacles, and a point S representing the sniffer dog's starting position. The goal is to determine the point F farthest from S within the grid that cannot be reached by a sniffer dog following a linear path. The solution involves identifying the convex hull of the grid's points of interest and then determining the point farthest from S within this hull. A sweeping line approach can be used to find the convex hull in O(n log n) time, where n is the number of points of interest. Once the convex hull is determined, the farthest point can be found by examining each hull point's distance from S and returning the point with the maximum distance. This overall process takes O(n log n) time. If the grid is massive and the query point S is a significant portion of the grid's size, a more efficient approach is necessary. In a 1D grid with obstacles and a point P compared to S, the farthest point from P is either directly adjacent or at the end of the grid. By transforming the grid into a 1D format with the smallest y-coordinate at the top and the largest y-coordinate at the bottom, the farthest point can be found in O(m) time, where m is the total number of points in the grid. This approach is more efficient for large grids but less practical for small grids due to the transformation process. In a grid with no obstacles, the farthest point from a given point is either directly adjacent or at the end of the grid. By transforming the grid into a 1D format with the smallest y-coordinate at the top and the largest y-coordinate at the bottom, the farthest point can be found in O(m) time, where m is the total number of points in the grid. If the grid has holes but the farthest point does not see them, the grid can be treated as a 1D grid with the largest y-coordinate at the top and the smallest y-coordinate at the bottom, and the farthest point can be found in O(m) time. If the grid has holes that the farthest point sees, the grid can be visualized as a 1D line with gaps, and the farthest point will be at the end of the line or directly adjacent to a gap. The grid's points of interest can be ordered based on their y-coordinates, and the farthest point will be the last point before a gap if a gap exists or the point with the largest distance from S if no gap

  that complements the TCP attack. This SRR regularizer is designed to enhance the resilience

At the sustainability stage, data and code should be maintained and updated regularly to ensure its continued use and relevance. The observed delay in thermalization was found to be directly proportional to the energy associated with the bias, thus indicating a causal relationship.  Theoretical models based on the Bogoliubov approach and the two-time non-equilibrium density matrix were utilized to simulate the situation and provide an explanation for the observed behavior.  The results showed that the delay is a manifestation of the sound wave that propagates through the gas in response to the disturbance, and it is anticipated that this phenomenon will occur in other non-equilibrium situations involving Bose gases.  The research also revealed that the relaxation time of the gas is of the same order as the time it takes for a sound wave to spread across the most significant dimension of the gas, which in this case was extremely small.  Consequently, the gas's thermalization time can be substantially reduced by increasing the energy associated with the disturbance or by introducing more complexity to the system, all without removing the non-equilibrium conditions.  This discovery is valuable for future experiments aiming to create non-equilibrium conditions in ultracold Bose gases and for the development of theoretical models for interacting gases in non-equilibrium situations.  Additionally, the study contributes to our understanding of how sound waves influence the behavior of ultracold Bose gases in unusual conditions, which is crucial for the design of experimental setups and the development of theoretical models.  The research also extends our knowledge of the dynamics of non-equilibrium Bose gases by showing that the Lagrange multipliers used to maintain non-equilibrium conditions propagate as sound waves through the gas, which is a novel and intriguing finding. This research investigates the dynamic behavior of adaptive patch attacks by training on previous successes, with the aim of understanding how they evolve over time and how they impact the accuracy of deep neural networks. We present a new type of vulnerability, which we call a pre-conditioned backdoor, allowing an eavesdropper to intercept quantum key distribution signals after the phase-matching condition is met. By deliberately introducing a pre-conditioned backdoor, we can reduce the key generation rate or an increase in noise, turning the system into a highly sensitive system that can be exploited for evil purposes. This pre-conditioned backdoor vulnerability enables an eavesdropper to access quantum key distribution signals after the phase-matching condition is met, allowing them to intercept the signals and threaten the security of the system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this pre-conditioned backdoor vulnerability can be implemented in various nonlinear optical processes, including second-harmonic generation, twin-photon entanglement, and spontaneous parametric down-conversion, thereby threatening the security of phase-matching based quantum key distribution systems based on these processes.  The pre-conditioned backdoor vulnerability contradicts commonly held beliefs that the boundless potential for variation in nonlinear optical processes precludes pre-designed vulnerabilities. It also undermines the idea that the phase-matching based quantum key distribution system is inherently secure, which has significant implications for its practical application and theoretical study.  To address this vulnerability, we propose an enhancement to the phase-matching quantum key distribution system by incorporating a wide-bandwidth ultrashort pulse laser, which can compensate for the fluctuations in the signal photon wavelength enabling true unconditional security.  We demonstrate that this optimized system can eliminate the pre-conditioned backdoor vulnerability and outperform traditional systems based on single-photon detectors by an order of magnitude.  Furthermore, we examine the practical application of this optimized system using ultrashort pulse lasers, which can reduce the key generation rate from several hundred kilometers to several tens of kilometers in the twin-photon entanglement based system, and from several thousands of kilometers to several hundreds of kilometers in the spontaneous parametric down-conversion based system.  It can also improve the system's sensitivity to the spontaneous parametric down-conversion by an order of magnitude and enable true unconditional security in the second-harmonic generation based system. Researchers have developed various methods to estimate effects when outcomes are either categorical or ordinal; however, they typically assume knowledge of the categories into which outcomes fall.  In reality, researchers often must determine these categories and compare the effects within them.  To address this common scenario, we develop a new inverse probability weight estimation approach that accounts for both categorical and ordinal outcomes.  This new method enables researchers to compare the effects within different categories or orderings of outcomes without a priori knowledge of these categories.  We demonstrate the application of this approach using microlevel data on damage to buildings and macrolevel data on the unemployment rate.  When compared to existing methods, our new approach offers improved accuracy when estimating treatment effects within different categories or orderings of outcomes.  We also extend our estimation approach to accommodate multiple groups receiving treatment and outcomes that exist along a continuum but are observed in discrete form.  Furthermore, our method is compatible with interaction terms, outcomes measured with error, and outcomes that vary over time.  We illustrate the utility of our new estimation approach using simulated data, data on the effects of job loss on psychological well-being, and data on the impact of demolition on building sale prices.  Our research contributes to the existing literature on treatment effects by providing a new estimation method that enables researchers to compare the effects of a treatment on outcomes that are either categorical or ordinal without a priori knowledge of how these outcomes are categorized or ordered.  This new method offers an alternative option for researchers who find that existing approaches cannot be applied to their research questions.  Additionally, our estimation approach is publicly available in the form of a user-friendly R package called "tins". Despite their impressive capabilities, PLMs are known to be susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can significantly impair their performance by manipulating their input.  This paper introduces the concept of targeted adversarial attacks aimed at plunging PLMs into a state of confusion, where common classifications become uncertain or undefined.  These unique attacks differ substantially from conventional attacks that strive to mislead PLMs into selecting an incorrect option from a predefined set of choices.  The researchers propose an innovative method for generating these enigmatic attacks, which leverages the underlying semantics of language as conveyed by parts-of-speech tags.  The proposed approach yields significantly better results compared to traditional methods, demonstrating its effectiveness across a range of PLMs and tasks.  The findings suggest that the underlying structure of natural language plays a crucial role in how PLMs process and classify information, underscoring the importance of considering linguistic semantics in the design of PLMs.  This research contributes to our understanding of how PLMs function and how they can be improved by incorporating linguistic principles during the training process.  The proposed approach also offers practical implications for developers seeking to create more robust and reliable NLP models. We present an approach to conducting sensitivity analysis with partially trusted data and a complex model that yields output in a highly processed form.  This method involves a three-step process:  (1) reverse-engineering the complex output to obtain a simpler intermediate value that reflects the variable's impact; (2) conducting a traditional sensitivity analysis on this intermediate value; and (3) validating the result by comparing the output from the complex model using partially trusted input with partially trusted output from the sensitivity analysis.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by conducting a sensitivity analysis on a climate model's temperature output in a region of interest (the Arctic) in response to varying CO2 levels.  Results show a significant discrepancy between the output from the complex model and the sensitivity analysis when applying a broad range of variables; however, when focusing on a specific process (sulfate aerosol impact on heat absorption in the Arctic) it yields similar results to the complex model's output and output from the full model with partially trusted input.  This approach offers a practical way for the community to validate complex models by comparing their output to results from simpler models or analytical studies; it also enables the evaluation of critical processes and variables that influence output uncertainty. This enhanced system's capacity to detect extremely low-level D-alpha emissions while avoiding saturation in areas of high emission allowed it to reveal plasma deuterium density peaks near the strike lines of the islands for the first time.  These peaks are essential factors in stabilizing the locked MHD mode by creating regions with stable orbitals, all while contributing to overall plasma confinement.  By enhancing the optical diagnostic observing D-alpha line emission system, researchers can gain a more precise understanding of plasma behavior in various scenarios, which is vital for developing and improving future fusion devices.   of other devices.  Furthermore, it's crucial to recognize that pulse
  oximetry's reliability can be compromised by factors such as motion,
  signal interference, and certain medical conditions, which may influence

  limitations and consider multiple measurement methods when making clinical
  decisions.  Ultimately, the choice of pulse oximeter should be based on its

MRI being a primary diagnostic tool, there is a growing need for automated analysis techniques to fully leverage its potential.  Given the high statistical power of large datasets, it is particularly crucial that these techniques be accurate and reliable.  In the context of left ventricular function assessment from Cardiac Cine MRI scans, this typically involves automated segmentation of images to frame by frame outline the heart's wall layers.  However, due to the high dimensionality of MRI volume data, this process can be extremely time-consuming and labor-intensive.  Furthermore, with the increasing number of patients and the limited availability of experts, traditional manual segmentation methods have reached their practical limitations.  Furthermore, the high standard required for clinical use due to the critical role that left ventricular function plays in diagnosis and treatment decisions further complicates the issue.  In this study, we investigate the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to improve automated MRI image segmentation accuracy and explore its clinical applicability by conducting frame-by-frame comparisons of proposed models with existing methods and statistically analyzing the results.  With a large dataset of 100 Cardiac Cine MRI scans and nearly 1000 volumes of data, we tested and compared the segmentation efficiency of traditional deep learning techniques such as 3D U-Net, 3D Res-DNN, and 3D Res-FCN alongside more advanced models like 3D Res-Attention-DNN and 3D Res-EGNet-FCN.  The results showed that the more complicated models required significantly more computational resources but yielded only minor improvements in segmentation accuracy.  Ultimately, the most effective model, 3D Res-Attention-DNN, demonstrated remarkably high accuracy rates of 99.2%, 98.4%, and 97.3% for epicardium, endocardium, and borderline segments respectively.  Furthermore, by applying this model to all slices of a representative scan and animating the resulting segmentations over time, we successfully visualized the left ventricular function in a highly detailed and realistic manner.  This research demonstrates the clinical viability of advanced AI algorithms for automated left ventricular function assessment from Cardiac Cine MRI scans and suggests that they meet the high standards required for clinical use.  As the largest study of its kind on this topic to date, it has significant implications for the development of practical AI-based segmentation tools and techniques.  Ultimately, by overcoming the primary obstacle to widespread automated image analysis, we believe that it paves the way for the full utilization of Cardiac Cine MRI scans

As healthcare data is diverse and comes from many sources, biases pre-existing in these data may inadvertently affect how AI-based systems perform and make decisions.  Furthermore, the presence of pre-existing biases in healthcare data means that training AI-based systems on such data risks embedding these biases and distorting legitimate patterns that the systems learn.  This pre-existing attribute of healthcare data that leads to biased outcomes when training AI-based systems is known as foundational bias.  Despite the significance of this issue, there is a lack of a unified framework in the healthcare domain to evaluate and mitigate foundational bias.  To address this gap, we propose a comprehensive framework that incorporates theoretical discussions, empirical analyses, and practical applications to tackle pre-existing biases in healthcare data.  This framework is designed to be versatile and applicable to various healthcare datasets and AI-based systems.  We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness by applying it to three distinct healthcare datasets (CT scans, medical texts, and audio signals) and show that it can efficiently identify pre-existing biases in these data.  Furthermore, the framework's ability to guide the collection of bias-free data makes it an invaluable tool for developing fair and legitimate patterns in AI-based systems.  By doing so, healthcare professionals and researchers can make informed decisions about designing and training these systems to produce unbiased outcomes.  The framework's availability on an open-source platform allows the healthcare community to build upon it and contribute to its development.  In summary, our comprehensive framework provides a unified approach to recognize, assess, mitigate, and prevent pre-existing biases in healthcare data that affect AI-based systems.  This framework has the potential to enhance the trustworthiness of these systems and promote their legitimate use in healthcare.  Healthcare professionals, researchers, developers, and policymakers can utilize this framework to advance the utilization of AI in healthcare by producing unbiased outcomes that prioritize health over other factors such as race, gender, age, and income. acy mechanisms to ensure that sufficient generation capacity is available to meet peak demand.  Historically, non-scheduled or reserve generation capacity has been a crucial component of such mechanisms.  However, with the integration of renewable energy sources like wind and solar power into these markets, the importance of reserve capacity has come into question.  Some research suggests that, due to the natural variability of renewable energy sources, higher levels of reserve capacity may be required.  Yet, other studies indicate that the inherent characteristics of renewable energy sources, combined with the existing market design, may actually reduce the necessary reserve capacity.  This research examines the theoretical basis for the calculation of reserve capacity, reviews the current market design, and analyzes the factors that influence reserve capacity requirements.  A key finding is that the way reserve capacity is defined and calculated contributes to the need for more of it when renewable energy sources are involved.  Furthermore, the research reveals that the existing marginal capacity approach to calculating reserve capacity is not efficient, as it does not account for the true value that reserve capacity provides to the market.  A more efficient alternative, known as the expected shortfall approach, is explored and found to yield better results when renewable energy sources are available but are not generating.  Ultimately, the study recommends that market designs be modified to better reflect the true value of reserve capacity and suggests that the expected shortfall approach be considered as an alternative.  By doing so, the research aims to help markets with significant renewable energy sources reduce the requirement for reserve capacity or remove the requirement altogether.  Additionally, the study proposes that research be conducted into even more efficient reserve capacity models that take into account the specific characteristics of individual renewable energy sources and the existing infrastructure of the market in question.  By optimizing reserve capacity requirements, the research strives to minimize costs while ensuring that generation capacity meets peak demand when non-scheduled or reserve generation capacity is not included in the total generation capacity available for market competition.  In this way, the study seeks to contribute to the development of more effective resource adequacy mechanisms that balance the needs of generators, consumers, and the market as a whole with the growing presence of renewable energy sources.  The research consists of five chapters.  Chapter one provides an introduction to the subject matter, outlining the purpose of the study, surveying the current state of reserve capacity requirements in liberalized electricity markets, and highlighting the research questions to be addressed.  Chapter two examines the theoretical basis for the calculation of reserve capacity, reviewing the existing marginal capacity approach and analyzing the factors that influence reserve capacity requirements

The effectiveness of a deep learning-based detection system in this scenario hinges
on the quality of the available training data. However, creating ScaneDCT-based 
scanner images suitable for training a neural network is impractical due to the

Moreover, even if creating these images was possible, storing them would be 
unfeasible within the memory constraints of conventional hardware. 
To address these obstacles, we propose an initialization method called 
ScaneDCT-Embedding and a new activation function called ActvSoft plus a set of 
modified convolutional neural network layers. These components enable the 
training of efficient anomaly detection systems using realistic simulator-based 
scanner images. 
Our solution offers significant benefits in terms of memory requirements and 
computational complexity compared to using regular initializers and activation 
functions. 
For example, when using a ScaneDCT scanner, we can reduce the parameters of the 
first convolutional neural network layer by as much as 75% and still maintain 
similar detection accuracy. 
Our proposed framework is highly adaptable and can be applied to various scanner 
models and configurations. 
It also outperforms existing solutions in terms of accuracy and efficiency in 
multiple scanner models and configurations.

While fractures generated by magma drive pressures are a common feature of small, airless bodies like asteroids and moons, they are relatively rare on larger planets like Earth and Ganymede.  One possible reason for this disparity is that fractures formed by diapiric magma drive pressures may take a long time to develop, which could explain their scarcity on larger bodies.  However, to determine if frictional sliding along fractures is a significant factor delaying their formation or making them less probable, we need to understand the dynamics of fracture growth in a realistic, gravitational environment.  To this end, we conducted 2D numerical simulations of fracture growth driven by pressurized magma diapirs, with various initial conditions and configurations.  These simulations allowed us to evaluate the effect of gravity on fracture growth dynamics by comparing results obtained using both a gravity-reduced model and a full, gravity-included model.  The outcomes of these simulations enabled us to develop a simplified theoretical model of fracture growth driven by magma diapirs, which can be applied to various scenarios and configurations.  One notable finding was that frictional sliding along fractures does not substantially delay their growth or make them less probable.  However, it does influence the shape and size of fractures by restricting growth to areas with lower stress.  Additionally, we discovered that the presence of gravity is crucial for creating wide, shallow fractures, which are common features observed on small, airless bodies.  By conducting simulations with different initial diapir sizes and shapes, we found that fractures develop more easily in areas with lower pressurization levels and grow faster in regions with higher stress.  To better understand these outcomes, we analyzed various factors influencing fracture growth dynamics, including stress concentration, diapir shape and size, gravity's effect, and frictional resistance.  Our results suggest that the scarcity of deep, wide fractures on larger planets like Earth and Ganymede could be attributed to factors such as lower pressurization levels and faster cooling rates, rather than the growth rate of fractures driven by magma diapirs.  Our research provides valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of fractures driven by magma diapirs, which can help improve our understanding of crustal structure development on small, airless bodies and possibly even rocky exoplanets.  Our numerical models and theoretical framework can be applied to various scenarios and configurations, which can be extended and modified to investigate other dynamic processes affecting fracture growth dynamics. While this test is widely used, it has several limitations, particularly when data sets are large or there are many observations. In such cases, conducting the test and determining a suitable alpha level can be computationally intensive and may not provide accurate results. Furthermore, many statistical software programs are not designed to directly calculate the p-value of the test, instead often returning a chi-squared value that requires an additional lookup to a distribution table to obtain a p-value. To address these challenges, we developed an enhanced version of the R function "spearman.rank" that calculates Spearman's rank correlation coefficient and conducts the associated test, enabling users to easily determine the presence of a significant rank correlation when alpha = 0.05. This updated function is part of the "DSAIDE" package, which aims to provide tools to help students learn about statistical tests and techniques by performing the tests themselves rather than simply looking up results in a textbook. By conducting the test and returning a straightforward "TRUE" or "FALSE" result indicating a significant rank correlation, users can better understand the underlying principles of the test and how it applies to real-data scenarios. Although this specific example involves a non-significant result, a notable characteristic of the test is its consistency with other tests that measure the strength of the relationship between variables, such as the Kendall's tau test. To facilitate the reproduction of the results, we attached the sample data sets to the manuscript.   A widespread technique for investigating this structure involves creating mutations at specified DNA bases
  and analyzing the resulting effects on protein function.
  Although developing mutations is a relatively straightforward process, determining the initial
  functional status of these bases is a more complex task.
  Currently, a commonly used reference standard, derived by BlDiscov (BlDiscov, a tool for determining
  contact distances between molecules), indicates that areas of a protein that contact other proteins
  or play a role in binding sites have an active, or "functional," status.
  However, our research shows that this standard is inaccurate for non-binding sites.
  BlDiscov incorrectly classifies bases that contribute crucially to enzyme activity, as seen in
  studies of the enzyme Maltodextrin glucosidase (MGD), a key decay regulator in potatoes.
  In one instance, a mutation altered a base that BlDiscov designated non-essential but actually
  affected the enzyme's functionality by disrupting a critical contact with a zinc ion.  
  This discovery highlights the need to replace the BlDiscov standard with more precise definitions
  for evaluating the structural significance of genetic information.  
  Our findings using the Maltodextrin glucosidase enzyme demonstrate that active sites require a more
  stringent standard than binding sites.  
  We propose two alternative metrics: contact distances (Discov) and atomic overlap (Overlap), and
  compare their effectiveness to BlDiscov by analyzing over 230,000 amino acid bases across nearly
  1,000 protein enzymes.

  Overlap standard is more precise but more computationally intensive.  
  The Discov standard is suitable for large-scale analyses but may yield false positives for bases
  involved in binding sites or other critical contacts.  
  The Overlap standard is more appropriate for in-depth analyses of specific proteins but is less
  widely supported by computational tools.  
  We provide both standard files on the BlDiscov website to facilitate replacement with more
  precise alternatives.

With the advent of machine learning techniques, there's growing interest in utilizing spectral data to detect counterfeit drugs.  While machine learning methods like support vector machines, random forests, and neural networks have shown promise in detecting counterfeit medicines based on spectral data, their effectiveness varies when applied to similar data sets.  To better understand how these methods compare when using spectral data to identify counterfeit drugs, we conducted an in-depth analysis of their performance using NIR spectral data collected from publicly available sources.  Our results show that the optimal model is not always the most complex or sophisticated, contradicting the common assumption in machine learning applications.  By thoroughly examining the performance of these methods across multiple data sets, we found that the best approach often depends on the quality of the spectral data.  When working with high-quality data, sophisticated models like neural networks tend to perform well; however, when dealing with noisy or low-quality data, simpler methods like support vector machines usually yield better results.  Our findings highlight the importance of balancing the complexity of machine learning models with the quality of the spectral data used to train them.  As the majority of spectral data is initially of poor quality and only refined through sophisticated processing techniques, the most effective model often turns out to be the simplest one - typically a linear regression model - before any data processing takes place.  By doing so, the best results are achieved when detecting counterfeit drugs based on spectral data, as demonstrated by our experiments.  Our research suggests that practitioners should avoid the preconception that sophisticated machine learning models are necessarily superior when utilizing spectral data to identify counterfeit drugs.  Instead, they should prioritize the most effective model for their particular data set, which may be a linear regression model if the initial data is of high quality, or a support vector machine if the data is noisy, as demonstrated by our R-squared values of 0.93 and 0.88 respectively.  Our findings have significant implications for developing practical and effective machine learning-based strategies for detecting counterfeit drugs, and our code is available on GitHub for others to use and build upon.  Our research contributes to the growing body of evidence that the best machine learning model for a given problem is not necessarily the most complex or sophisticated one, but rather the one that yields the best results by minimizing the error between predicted and actual values.  This research also adds to the body of evidence that the quality of spectral data precedes the quality of models when detecting counterfeit drugs,

By analyzing these data, we determined the atmospheric composition of the star at the time of observation.  Using a spectrum taken 20 years ago as a reference, we found that helium and nitrogen emissions increased significantly during the outburst.  A new emission line from Sulfur (S II) was also detected, indicating that the star had entered a phase of massive mass loss.  These findings are consistent with the behavior of similar LBV stars, such as Rho Dor and P Cygni, and support the hypothesis that these stars explode as supernovae at the end of their life cycle.  Furthermore, the data suggests that Eta Scoriae Australis is a massive star with a low initial metallicity, based on the presence of N II emissions and the lack of O I emissions.  The observation that Sulfur emissions are common in LBV stars that explode as supernovae, but rare in those that do not, provides a possible indicator for distinguishing between these types of stars.  Ultimately, the research contributes to our understanding of the Physical Processes that shape the spectra of LBV stars during outburst, as well as our knowledge of the Atmospheric Composition and Mass Loss Behavior of these enigmatic objects.  The detection of Sulfur emissions in Eta Scoriae Australis also raises interesting questions about the Star Formation History of the Scorpio-Centaurus OB1 complex.  The data collected in this study is publicly available to the scientific community, along with a set of pre-formed spectra that can be used for educational purposes.  The observation that Eta Scoriae Australis is losing mass at a rate of approximately 10^-5 solar masses per year suggests that the star is approaching the end of its life cycle, during which it is expected to explode as a supernova.  However, the star's distance from Earth makes it difficult to predict when this event will occur, although it is believed to happen within the next few thousand years.  The research highlights the importance of continued monitoring of the star's behavior, as well as the recovery of historical spectra, which can provide valuable information about the star's condition and the conditions under which it was observed.
