This research presents an advanced technique for identifying events with missing transverse momentum by improving upon existing methods, and applies this technique to search for a dark sector through the dark photon mediator in events with beauty b-jets at the Large Hadron Collider.  A dark sector model that includes dark electrons, dark photons, and dark mesons is searched for using 13.6 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions collected at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV.  In the scenario where a dark photon decays into a standard electron and a dark electron, and a dark meson decays into two dark electrons, no significant excess is found over the standard model expectations.  This research sets the most stringent limits to date on the dark photon mass, requiring it to be greater than 12.6 GHz, and places constraints on the dark electron charge, requiring it to be less than 0.06%.  Additionally, a search is conducted for a dark sector that includes dark quarks in events with beauty b-jets at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TEv, with no significant excess found over the standard model expectations.  This research sets the most stringent limits to date on the dark gluon force scale, requiring it to be greater than 870 MeV.  This research also contributes to the development of search strategies for New Physics through the inclusion of a dark sector that includes dark quarks in the dark hadronization model.  This research is the most comprehensive search to date for a dark sector through the dark photon mediator in events with beauty b-jets at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TEv.    Missing transverse momentum events can be categorized into true and false events.  True events represent signals of New Physics, whereas false events are standard model backgrounds that masquerade as true events.  True events usually exhibit distinct characteristics that differentiate them from false events.  However, the most effective way to identify these characteristics is through the most significant jet pair in events with missing transverse momentum.  A new technique called $p_T^\text{min}$ has been developed to supplement existing methods.  This research applies the $p_T^\text{min}$ technique to search for a dark sector through the dark photon mediator in events with beauty b-jets at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TEv.  No significant excess is found over the standard model expectations.

Recent studies have discovered a substantial number of pre-trained language models exhibit biased performance on certain linguistic patterns, including negative language and semantic similarity.  These findings are intriguing because they deviate from what is expected from models meeting the high standards of generalization theory.  Furthermore, research has revealed that pre-trained models can learn to recognize negative language within a limited scope of similarity, but extendning the range of similarity leads to impaired performance.  This paper introduces a new hypothesis - that pre-trained models succeed with negatively phrased queries due to pattern-based techniques used during training, rather than true semantic understanding.  This hypothesis is supported by experimental results demonstrating that eliminating pattern-based methods during fine-tuning leads to improved performance on negatively phrased queries with similar similarity levels.  Additionally, we observe that pre-trained models excel at recognizing negatively phrased patterns in raw data but struggle to do so with naturally occurring language, as evident from poor performance on naturally occurring negatively phrased sentences and high scores for artificially created ones.  Overall, our research suggests that pre-trained models perceive negatively phrased queries with difficulty, hampering their capacity to learn from them effectively.  This discovery carries implications for both theory and practice, contributing to our comprehension of how pre-trained models process language and providing direction for developing generalization guidelines.  We also offer a new evaluation method - negatively phrased semantic similarity - that researchers can utilize to assess the intrinsic properties of pre-trained models before employing them in various applications.  Furthermore, we present three actionable suggestions for improving generalization by promoting natural occurrence of negatively phrased training data during pre-training, fine-tuning, and within regular language, and offer raw data and codes on publicly available repositories for replication purposes.  These strategies have the potential to enhance performance on negatively phrased queries, as verified through experimental results on three pre-trained models (T5, PaLM, and Llama) and two pre-trained models from Google (LGMT5 and LGMT-L) along with publicly available pre-trained models on pre-trained models on sentiment analysis and natural language generation on e-commerce descriptions available on the web.  Additionally, we include pre-processing scripts on publicly available repositories for replication purposes.  We hope our research inspires further investigation into the subject matter.  One limitation of our research is the focus on pre-trained models available today, constraining the scope of negatively phrased patterns that we could examine. Such a property makes traditional graph theory inadequate for analyzing and understanding the behavior of interest-based search mechanisms within these systems.  In response, the concept of a time-varying graph is introduced and its topology characterized.  Counterintuitive patterns of interest distribution often lead to the formation of bubbles in search outcomes.  To better understand these patterns, we need to grasp the basic properties of the graph that drives them.  Two specific instances of faulty topology are identified - a cycle that contributes to the creation of a search bubble and a condition where multiple interests share a common cause but are isolated from each other.  These irregularities complicate the optimization of search results but do not preclude legitimate distribution patterns among nodes.  These irregularities are rare and only appear in graphs where specific topological conditions are met.  More precisely, a necessary and sufficient condition for a graph to contain a cycle that generates a search bubble is proposed.  Two different metrics for evaluating the complexity of a graph's topology are introduced and their practical applications outlined.  The purpose of these metrics is to determine if the native search outcome reflects the genuine interests of nodes or if more sophisticated search strategies are required.  These metrics can also be utilized to analyze other dynamic information dispersal processes within closed systems.  Closed systems where nodes share distinct and irreducible interests serve as the initial configuration in many distributed computing models.  These models include population protocols, opportunistic networking, and sensor networks.  The absence of a cycle in this topology guarantees that the most privileged interest of each node is unique.  This uniqueness ensures the effectiveness of basic search mechanisms.  An example of a time-varying graph that consistently produces isolated nodes in search outcomes is presented.  This graph contains no cycles but multiple interests within it are not genuinely distinct. This paper introduces an adaptive learning rate schedule for neural-equipped reinforcement learning algorithms that tackles the high costs associated with exploring unknown areas of the state-space.  The proposed 'Region-Adaptive' schedule adjusts the learning rate based on the difference between the current and maximum values seen so far for a given state, all while leveraging a suitable initial exploration strategy. We examine the SNe-Ia explosion mechanics and its impact on the gravitational wave signal, focusing on the conditions under which an explosion could occur before the massive star collides with the neutron star.  Using a first-in-order approximation, we calculate the gravitational wave signals emitted during the approach and merger phases of the binary system, consisting of a normal star and a neutron star, with the possibility of an SNe-IA explosion.  We find that, in the case of a direct SNe-IA explosion, the signal is too weak to be detected by current gravitational wave detectors.  However, if the massive star's explosion precedes its collision with the neutron star, resulting in a delayed SNe-IA explosion, the signal becomes significant enough to be detectable by future detectors, allowing for the possibility of verifying the theory through observation.
